title: Kevin of Glendalough (3 June)
hook: an Irish hermit who, legend says, held still while a blackbird nested in his hand

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Visitation: Mary hurrying over the hills to her cousin Elizabeth. Your line was she went in haste.

A stone cell in a wooded Irish valley. A man kneels inside, praying, one arm stretched out through the small window, palm up, still as a branch. A blackbird lands on the open hand. She looks around. She starts to bring twigs, one at a time. Yesterday was all haste. Today, an Irish saint whose story is about not moving at all. Kevin of Glendalough.
screen: `A STONE CELL IN A VALLEY.` → `AN ARM THROUGH THE WINDOW.` → `A BLACKBIRD LANDS.`

segments.voice: Start with what is history and what is legend. Kevin was a hermit and a monk in Ireland, and the monastery that grew up around him in the valley of Glendalough is remembered as his. The blackbird comes from the legend, written down long after his time by medieval writers including Gerald of Wales. Kevin was praying with one hand stretched out through the window of his cell, and a blackbird built a nest in his upturned palm and laid her eggs there. Kevin did not pull his hand back. Tradition says he held it there, patient, until the eggs hatched and the young birds flew. Nobody has to believe a man held his arm out that long to hear what the story is saying. It's a picture of prayer as staying. Not getting something done, but being so still that a living thing can trust you with its future. The psalm says it in one line. In the Douay-Rheims: "Be still and see that I am God." Kevin's hand is that line made into a scene. Notice what the story counts as holy. Not a miracle Kevin performs, but a small bird's ordinary work, nest and eggs and feeding, which he refuses to interrupt. In stories like this one, animals are neighbors in God's world. Jesus points at birds too. "Behold the birds of the air," he says, and reminds his listeners that their heavenly Father feeds them. Kevin does more than look. He becomes the place the bird is fed. And holding still costs something. An arm gets tired. A plan gets canceled. Some readers hear the story as being about anyone who stays put for someone else's sake: a parent by a crib, a nurse by a bed, a friend who doesn't leave the room.
screen: `HISTORY: A HERMIT IN A VALLEY.` · `LEGEND: A NEST IN HIS OPEN HAND.` · `PRAYER AS STAYING.` · `HOLDING STILL COSTS SOMETHING.` · then, large: `BE STILL AND SEE THAT I AM GOD.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your knee, palm up and open, gripping nothing, a place where something could land. When you want to shift, notice the wanting, and stay a little longer. If you pray, say the psalm's line once, slowly, be still and see that I am God; if you don't, let the open hand be enough.
Kevin, the Irish hermit of Glendalough. Legend says he held his hand still until a blackbird's young had flown.
Your line: the blackbird. Staying put for someone can be its own kind of prayer. Rest well.

howItsDone: Saint Kevin is remembered on 3 June, above all in Ireland; pilgrims visit the monastic site at Glendalough, and the blackbird story is often told or shown in pictures of him.
